name: Beef
notes:
Beef, nutrition from USDA. This is world-average beef, which includes a large share from grazing systems on cleared tropical land: cattle ranching drives most Amazon deforestation.

Emissions come from Poore & Nemecek's global average (~99 kg CO2e/kg), split into methane (~1.9 kg), nitrous oxide and direct CO2, with feed counted separately. The US is far lower: methane, nitrous oxide and energy are from Rotz et al. 2019 and the EPA inventory, because US beef is mostly feedlot-finished and grows faster. Grazing land is large (0.015 ha/kg world; US 0.037 from Eshel 2014). Feed is mostly corn, plus soy, alfalfa, hay and sorghum.

The neuron count (9.3 billion) is estimated from a cow's 480 g brain, using counts from related hoofed animals. It was raised from 3 billion on 2026-10-01. Several older world values (weight 500 kg, 43% meat yield, world grazing land) have no recorded derivation in their notes.
land_types_note: Mostly grassland pasture and feed crops, but cattle ranching drives most Amazon deforestation and much Cerrado clearing.

source.note: Beef — pasture_ha_per_kg_output (US): Eshel et al. 2014 (USDA data 2000–2010) put total US land for animal-based food at ~3.7 million km2, with beef pasture ~79% of that (~2.92 million km2 = ~292 Mha). Divided by US beef production ~26 billion lb carcass weight/yr (~11.8 Mt CW, USDA 2000–2010 average) = ~0.0247 ha/kg CW. Converted to boneless retail basis (same as existing world entry; yield_fraction 0.43 of live weight) with CW-to-retail factor 0.67 (Rotz et al. 2019: ~33% fat, bone and shrink loss): 0.0247 / 0.67 ≈ 0.037 ha/kg. Cross-check: USDA ERS Major Land Uses 2017 grassland pasture+range (~265 Mha) plus grazed forest (~53 Mha) ≈ 318 Mha, ~90% beef-grazed, over ~11.9 Mt CW gives ~0.024 ha/kg CW, consistent. US value exceeds the world entry because much US beef grazing is on low-productivity arid western rangeland. US.

source.note: Beef — n2o_kg_per_kg_output (US): US EPA GHG Inventory 2024, year 2022. Manure management N2O for beef cattle (direct + indirect, Table 5-7) = 24 kt. Plus direct N2O from manure/urine deposited on pasture, range and paddock (PRP, Table 5-17): 13.8 MMT CO2e / 265 = 52.1 kt N2O for all grazing species; beef share assumed ~85% (beef cattle not on feed are by far the dominant PRP animals; dairy mostly confined; sheep/horses/goats/bison minor) = 44.3 kt. Total ≈ 68.3 kt N2O. Excludes feed-crop fertilizer N2O and managed manure applied to cropland. Divided by ~11.96 Mt CW from beef-category cattle (28.3 billion lb commercial beef 2022 minus ~0.9 Mt dairy cull cows) = 5.7 g N2O/kg CW; converted to boneless retail basis with CW-to-retail factor 0.67 (Rotz et al. 2019) = 8.5 g ≈ 0.0085 kg N2O/kg. Sanity check: Rotz et al. 2019 total beef N2O is 19.9 g/kg CW but that includes feed-crop fertilizer N2O. Confidence 2 because the PRP beef share is an assumption. US.

source.title: Rotz et al. (2019) — Environmental footprints of beef cattle production in the United States (Agricultural Systems)
source.note: Beef — co2_kg_per_kg_output (US): Rotz et al. 2019 Table 2 US beef-breed farm-gate energy use per kg carcass weight: fuel 0.25 L × ~2.7 kg CO2/L (EPA diesel factor) = 0.675; natural gas 0.03 m3 × ~1.94 kg CO2/m3 = 0.058; electricity 0.41 kWh × ~0.43 kg CO2/kWh (EPA eGRID US average, ~2018) = 0.176; total ≈ 0.91 kg CO2/kg CW. Excludes land-use change (the world entries include an LUC residual, so the large gap is partly a scope difference). US.

name: Chicken
notes:
Broiler chicken, nutrition from USDA. Chicken's neuron count is a measured value (221 million, isotropic fractionator), one of the few direct counts in the dataset. Each bird weighs ~2.5 kg at slaughter, with 75% usable meat.

Feed (~2.1 kg per kg meat) is corn, soy, wheat and sorghum, so almost all of chicken's land is cropland for feed, including some Brazilian soy. Emissions: on-farm manure methane and nitrous oxide (Poore & Nemecek and GLEAM agree), plus Poore & Nemecek's post-farm stages (processing, transport, retail, packaging, losses). Before 2026-09-26 only on-farm energy was counted. An older unit error stored nitrous oxide as CO2e; that was fixed on 2026-06-04.

No pasture. The weight note in the data was copied from the neuron note, so the 2.5 kg weight has no recorded derivation.
land_types_note: Almost all land is corn/soy feed: mostly temperate grassland farmland, with the soy share partly from Brazil's Cerrado and Amazon edges.

name: Pork
notes:
Pork, nutrition from USDA. Pig neuron count is a measured value (~2.2 billion, Kazu et al. 2014), one of the few direct counts. The pig in that study was young; neuron numbers are mostly set early in life, so it's used for market pigs (~90 kg at slaughter, 70% meat yield).

Feed is corn, soy and wheat. Emissions: on-farm methane and nitrous oxide come from Poore & Nemecek's farm stage, split using GLEAM's pig shares (mostly manure methane). That was fixed on 2026-09-26: before, they added up to ~5× Poore & Nemecek's farm total. Post-farm stages (processing, transport, retail, packaging, losses) were added the same day.

No pasture, since most pigs are housed.

Some vitamins come from a stand-in USDA record (cooked ground pork), scaled to raw.
land_types_note: Almost all land is corn/soy feed: mostly temperate grassland farmland, with the soy share partly from Brazil's Cerrado and Amazon edges.

name: Venison (Wild)
notes:
Wild white-tailed deer, as hunted in North America. Nutrition from USDA raw venison: very lean.

There's no farmland, feed or pasture, because the deer live on land that exists anyway. Land use is zero, and the scorer treats zero as a perfect score on that measure. It's tagged 'wild', so the Over-Hunting slider divides its score, to account for limited wild supply. Methane is the deer's own digestion (~3.5 kg per deer per year, Felton 2014). CO2 is mostly hunters driving to and from the hunt.

No deer brain has been counted. The 5.0 billion neurons are estimated from a ~200 g brain using counts from related hoofed animals (raised from 1.7 billion on 2026-10-01). Deer are ~70 kg live with ~50% boneless meat. Availability is FAOSTAT 'game meat' (all species, so an upper bound for venison).

Some vitamins come from a stand-in USDA record (broiled deer loin).

source.note: Venison (Wild) — ch4_kg_per_kg_output: Raw kg CH4 per kg venison (multiply by GWP100=28 for CO2e). White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) are ruminants producing enteric CH4. Felton et al. (2014) synthesise cervid CH4 data and estimate emission factors of 2–5 kg CH4/animal/year for mid-sized deer (40–80 kg body mass), with a central estimate of ~3.5 kg CH4/animal/year for a 70 kg deer on a natural browse diet. At 70 kg live weight with 50% yield fraction = 35 kg venison per harvest: 3.5 / 35 = 0.10 kg CH4/kg venison. No manure management CH4 applies — wild deer defecate freely across the landscape. 0.10 × 28 = 2.8 kg CO2e/kg, substantially below managed beef (53.2 CO2e) and lamb (15.3 CO2e) due to absence of feedlot manure management and lower annual enteric output per unit meat from single-harvest wild animals.

For white-tailed deer at 70 kg body mass: IPCC default ~3.3 kg CH4/animal/year. At 35 kg edible yield per animal: 3.3 / 35 = 0.094 kg CH4/kg ≈ 0.095. Consistent with Felton et al. (2014) central estimate and confirms the 0.10 value. Confidence 3 — IPCC defaults for wild cervids carry higher uncertainty than livestock-specific values.

source.note: Venison (Wild) — n2o_kg_per_kg_output: Wild deer produce no attributable concentrated manure N2O — excreta are dispersed across native ecosystems rather than collected, stored, or applied to cropland. Trace N2O arises from distributed dung and urine patches on soil, but this is part of the natural nitrogen cycle and is not attributable to the harvest production system. A residual value of 0.001 kg N2O/kg (corresponding to ~0.27 kg CO2e/kg at GWP100=265) is assigned to account for negligible hunter transport and processing N2O, consistent with IPCC Tier 1 methodology for wild game. Confidence 2 — no direct measurement; value is a lower-bound estimate.

source.note: Venison (Wild) — co2_kg_per_kg_output: Direct CO2 from hunting and processing activities. This excludes upstream ecosystem CH4 (captured in ch4 field) and is well below farmed beef CO2 (~14.6 kg/kg) because there is no feed crop production, no feedlot energy, and no industrial slaughter chain. Confidence 2 — wild game CO2 is highly variable by hunt distance and local infrastructure.

notes:
Wild eastern grey squirrel, as hunted in North America. Nutrition from USDA raw squirrel.

Like venison, there's no farmland, feed or pasture, so land use is zero. It's tagged 'wild' for the Over-Hunting slider. A squirrel weighs ~0.5 kg with ~40% meat, so about 5 squirrels die per kg of meat. Its estimated 450 million neurons (rodent brain-size scaling; no direct count) make it the highest sentient harm per kg of any land animal here. That's why it ranks near the bottom.

CO2 is mostly hunter driving, spread over very little meat per trip. Availability (5 Gg) is a placeholder guess with no data behind it (confidence 1). It should be replaced if a real figure turns up.

notes:
Duck meat, nutrition from USDA roasted duck (meat only). China produces about 80% of the world's duck meat.

name: Beef Liver
notes:
Raw beef liver, nutrition from USDA (FDC 169451). Liver is very high in vitamin A and B12, which gives it a very high nutrition score.

Everything else is copied from beef: emissions, land, water, feed and the animal figures. That treats a kg of liver as having the same footprint and animal harm as a kg of beef meat, rather than giving it a smaller share because it is a low-value byproduct of the same animal. source.note: Beef — n2o_kg_per_kg_output (US): US EPA GHG Inventory 2024, year 2022. Manure management N2O for beef cattle (direct + indirect, Table 5-7) = 24 kt. Plus direct N2O from manure/urine deposited on pasture, range and paddock (PRP, Table 5-17): 13.8 MMT CO2e / 265 = 52.1 kt N2O for all grazing species; beef share assumed ~85% (beef cattle not on feed are by far the dominant PRP animals; dairy mostly confined; sheep/horses/goats/bison minor) = 44.3 kt. Total ≈ 68.3 kt N2O. Excludes feed-crop fertilizer N2O and managed manure applied to cropland. Divided by ~11.96 Mt CW from beef-category cattle (28.3 billion lb commercial beef 2022 minus ~0.9 Mt dairy cull cows) = 5.7 g N2O/kg CW; converted to boneless retail basis with CW-to-retail factor 0.67 (Rotz et al. 2019) = 8.5 g ≈ 0.0085 kg N2O/kg. Sanity check: Rotz et al. 2019 total beef N2O is 19.9 g/kg CW but that includes feed-crop fertilizer N2O. Confidence 2 because the PRP beef share is an assumption. US.

name: Bison
notes:
Bison (buffalo), as raised on North American rangeland, nutrition from USDA raw lean bison. Very little is measured, so most of this entry is educated guesses at confidence 1.

A bison is slaughtered at ~520 kg live and ~2.3 years, ~41% boneless meat (~213 kg; 58% dressing × ~70% boneless; estimates). Methane uses eddy-covariance measurements of 52–81 g of CH4 per bison a day (less than cattle); I used 81 g/day = 30 kg a year, over ~3.4 animal-years per slaughtered animal (2.3 years growing plus ~1.1 cow-years of breeding herd), ≈ 0.47 kg CH4 per kg of meat. Nitrous oxide (0.012) and CO2 (1.4) are guesses near US beef's values.

Bison graze rangeland that's mostly not cropland, but it takes a lot of it: ~4 ha per animal-year over ~3.4 animal-years is ~0.065 ha per kg of meat (more than beef's 0.015 world and 0.037 US). Some animals are grain-finished, so a little corn and alfalfa feed is charged. The neuron count reuses the cattle estimate (no bison brain mass was found). Availability: ~80,000 US (2023) and ~41,000 Canadian (2024) bison a year ≈ 30 Gg of meat.
land_types_note: Northern and central Great Plains grassland in the US and the Canadian prairies.

name: Rabbit
notes:
Farmed rabbit meat (domestic rabbit, raised indoors on pellets), nutrition from USDA raw rabbit. Rabbit is one of the few meats with published life-cycle assessments: 7.6–10.5 kg CO2e per kg of carcass (about 2.6–3.9 per kg live weight), with feed making up ~70%. The benchmark emissions here take the 9.0 midpoint per kg of carcass ÷ 0.8 boneless share = ~11.2 kg CO2e per kg of meat.

A rabbit is slaughtered at ~2.5 kg live and ~11 weeks; the dressed carcass is ~58% and ~80% of that is boneless meat, so ~0.46 of live weight is meat (estimates). Feed is ~9.4 kg per kg of boneless meat (feed conversion of ~3.5 kg per kg of live weight plus the breeding does' feed, roughly 4.4 kg per kg live ÷ 0.46), split over alfalfa, wheat (bran), corn and soy (confidence 1). The methane, nitrous oxide and CO2 figures are back-solved so the on-farm part (~5.6 kg CO2e) plus feed lands near the LCA benchmark; they are not measurements. The neuron count (~1 billion) is a rough estimate from a ~11 g brain at rodent-like neuron densities, since no rabbit count was found. No pasture. Availability is FAOSTAT's rabbit meat.
land_types_note: Almost all land is corn/soy feed: mostly temperate grassland farmland, with the soy share partly from Brazil's Cerrado and Amazon edges.
